lead: A VR system is not one device. It is four parts working as one loop: input devices that sense the user, output devices that stimulate the senses, a computer that runs the world model and simulation, and the human at the end of both. The human is a part because human senses set the requirements. Designers use this split to budget cost, find the weak link and debug an experience. A cheap phone viewer and a laboratory CAVE both contain the same four parts; only the hardware and software inside each part change.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the terms and 1.4 for the closed loop these parts implement.

sections.h3: Four parts in one closed loop

blocks.text: Every VR system has four parts. Input devices sense what the user does: head turn, hand position, button press, spoken command. Output devices stimulate the user's senses: eyes, ears, skin and muscles. The computer and software hold a model of the virtual world and update it. The human is the fourth part, because the loop closes through a person.

The split is practical. If a training simulation feels wrong, the fault can sit in any part: a tracker that drifts, a display that lags, a physics engine that lets a virtual cup pass through a table, or a task that asks the eyes to do work they cannot do. Naming the four parts turns a vague complaint into a checklist.

The human belongs on the list because human limits set the requirements. A display must update fast enough that the eye reads motion as continuous. A sound must arrive close enough in time to the picture that the brain binds them. A haptic device must push back within the range a hand can feel. The interface is matched to human limits, not the other way round. This closed loop is the difference between VR and ordinary 3D graphics, as 1.4 explains.
Head-mounted displays, haptic devices and the inside of trackers are taken apart later. Here each part gets a name and a role.

Input devices fall into three groups. 3D position trackers measure where a body part is and how it is oriented. The main types are mechanical (linked arms), magnetic (coils in a field), ultrasonic (sound pulses), optical (cameras and markers) and inertial (accelerometers and gyroscopes). Data gloves and gesture input devices measure finger bend and hand shape. Navigation and manipulation interfaces let the user move and act: 3D mice, joysticks, wands and voice commands. Unit 2 covers how each works.

Output devices also fall into three groups. Graphics displays give the eyes a stereo image. Personal displays are worn on the head, such as a head-mounted display (HMD). Large-volume displays surround the user, such as a CAVE (a room whose walls are screens), a dome, or a wall. Sound displays give the ears spatial audio, so a virtual sound can come from the left or above. Haptic displays give the skin and muscles force or vibration: a glove that resists your fingers, a controller that shakes, a tool that pushes back. Unit 3 covers optics, spatial audio and haptic rendering.

The output set decides how many senses are engaged. A phone viewer engages sight and sound. A CAVE engages sight over a wide field and can add sound. A haptic rig adds touch and force. More output channels usually mean more immersion, but only if each channel is fast and consistent with the others.

sections.h3: The computer and the software half

blocks.text: The computer is the part that holds and changes the virtual world. Its software has four jobs.
World model or scene database. This stores what exists: objects, their shapes, colours, positions, materials and links. A virtual classroom might store 30 desks, a board and a teacher avatar.

Simulation engine. This applies rules and physics and updates state. If the user pushes a virtual box, the engine computes the new position, checks collisions and decides whether the box slides or stops. It also runs scripted behaviour, such as a door opening when a hand touches it.

Rendering engine. This draws the world from the user's current viewpoint. It takes the world model and the tracked head and hand data and produces the left and right eye images, the sound mix and, where present, haptic signals.

VR toolkit or game engine. This ties the pieces together: it loads the scene, connects tracker drivers, schedules the simulation step, calls the renderer and handles input events. Some syllabi call the software half the virtual world generator, because it generates the world the user experiences.

The parts run in a loop. Read trackers, update simulation, render, send output, repeat. If one stage is slow, the whole loop misses its deadline and the user feels lag. The figure shows the layers from application down to hardware.

figure.caption: The worked example as a loop: the phone is the computer and software, the viewer and phone screen give output, the gamepad and the phone's sensor are input, and the student is the human, with the parts totalling ₹17,500. Output is the weak link — a narrow field of view, no haptics, and only 3 DoF of head tracking, so leaning forward changes nothing.

spec.title: The student's ₹17,500 loop
spec.aria: A closed loop of four boxes: input devices (gamepad and 3-DoF phone sensor), the computer and software (the ₹15,000 phone), output devices (₹1,000 viewer and phone screen), and the human student, with arrows carrying head pose, images and sound, and the user's actions back to input; the output box is picked out as the weak link.

examples.question: A student builds a low-cost VR setup. A cardboard viewer costs ₹1,000, a mid-range phone costs ₹15,000, and a Bluetooth gamepad costs ₹1,500. The phone's inertial sensor tracks head orientation in 3 degrees of freedom (DoF): yaw, pitch and roll. A full 6-DoF tracker would also track position. (a) Name the four parts of a VR system and map each item to a part. (b) Find the total cost. (c) Find the number of degrees of freedom missing. (d) Which part limits immersion, and why?
steps: Four parts: input devices, output devices, computer and software, and the human.
Map: viewer = output; phone = computer and software, plus output (screen and speaker) and input (inertial sensor); gamepad = input; student = human.
Missing DoF = 6 − 3 = 3 position axes (x, y, z).
Limiting part: output. The phone screen gives a narrow field of view and no haptics; the tracker also lacks position, so leaning forward does not change the view.
examples.answer: Total cost is ₹17,500, 3 DoF are missing, and the output part limits immersion in this setup.
examples.check:
viewer = 1000
phone = 15000
gamepad = 1500
total = viewer + phone + gamepad
tracked = 3
needed = 6
missing = needed - tracked
print(total)
print(missing)

traps: Calling the headset the whole VR system. Marks are for input, output, computer/software and the human.
Forgetting the software half: the world model and simulation engine are part of the system, not optional extras.
Mixing input and output: a tracker is input; a haptic glove that pushes back is output, while a data glove that senses finger bend is input.
Treating the human as outside the system. Human senses set update rate, field of view and force limits.
Saying more sensors always means more immersion. A 3-DoF orientation tracker cannot give positional lean, and missing output channels cap immersion too.

quiz.q: List the four parts of a VR system.
quiz.a: Input devices, output devices, computer and software, and the human.

quiz.q: Why is the human counted as a component of the VR system?
quiz.a: Because the loop closes through the human, and human visual, auditory and haptic limits set the requirements for update rate, latency, field of view and force range.

quiz.q: A setup has a 4-DoF tracker: 3 orientation axes and 1 position axis. How many DoF are missing from full 6-DoF tracking?
quiz.a: Full tracking needs 6 DoF: 3 position and 3 orientation. The setup has 3 orientation and 1 position, so 2 position axes are missing. Answer: 2 DoF.

quiz.q: In a CAVE, a trainee sees a virtual ball hit a wall but hears the impact 200 ms later. Which component is at fault, and why?
quiz.a: The output side, specifically sound timing against graphics timing, or the runtime that schedules both. The human brain binds sight and sound only within a short window, so a 200 ms mismatch breaks the illusion. Fix the timing in the runtime and sound output, not the world model.

quiz.q: Name the three groups of input devices in a VR system.
quiz.a: 3D position trackers; data gloves and gesture input devices; navigation and manipulation interfaces such as 3D mice, joysticks, wands and voice.

quiz.q: What does the simulation engine do that the rendering engine does not?
quiz.a: The simulation engine applies rules and physics and updates the state of the world. The rendering engine draws that state from the user's viewpoint. Simulation decides what happens; rendering decides how it looks and sounds.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry splits the same four parts across OpenXR runtimes, game engines such as Unity and Unreal, and haptic middleware; the split helps teams divide work. Research on foveated rendering, inside-out tracking and wearable haptics changes the hardware layer, not the four-part model. Digital twins and teleoperation add a real sensor stream to the input side. Search for OpenXR, WebXR, scene graph, haptic rendering and motion-to-photon latency to go deeper.
